Native Hawaiian (Kānaka Maoli)

Begin with annotated public sources on Native Hawaiian identity, language education, land and water care, institutional roles and the 1993 federal apology. This initial source guide supports a Hawaiʻi map connection while keeping its limited coverage visible.

Names & relationshipsNative Hawaiian / Kānaka Maoli is a people-level access point, distinct from the population of the modern state and from any single agency or organization. OHA is a state agency; ʻAha Pūnana Leo and Paepae o Heʻeia are specific community institutions. The historical Kingdom, its subjects, Indigenous identity, ancestry-based program categories and contemporary political proposals require their own contexts. The state-index connection does not decide recognition, citizenship or territorial claims.
A source guide for a deeper dive.This entry provides a brief orientation and an organized reading path. A comprehensive deep dive has not yet been completed. Follow the annotated sources and distinguish primary community accounts from outside reference material.
01

An Indigenous people and a Hawaiian name

Native Hawaiian and Kānaka Maoli identify the Indigenous people of Hawaiʻi. The university naming reference provides an attributed introduction. The 1993 resolution uses an ancestry-based definition specific to that instrument; it is not a universal enrollment rule.

Read the sources [5] University of Hawaiʻi System News [4] United States Statutes at Large, 107 Stat. 1510–1514; Government Publishing Office / GovInfo

02

A homeland connection for the map

The resolution connects Native Hawaiian ancestors with the islands now indexed as Hawaiʻi. This state route is a finding aid, not a parcel map or a decision on territorial rights. Island-specific histories need further research.

Read the sources [4] United States Statutes at Large, 107 Stat. 1510–1514; Government Publishing Office / GovInfo

03

The Kingdom, overthrow and a dated apology

Congress’s 1993 resolution acknowledges United States involvement in the 1893 overthrow and apologizes to Native Hawaiians. It explicitly does not settle claims. Original Kingdom documents and Hawaiian scholarship are needed for a fuller history.

Read the sources [4] United States Statutes at Large, 107 Stat. 1510–1514; Government Publishing Office / GovInfo

04

Rebuilding everyday language education

ʻAha Pūnana Leo traces its work to Hawaiian language educators who organized in 1983. Its account describes the first preschool at Kekaha, Kauaʻi, in 1984, followed by schools on other islands. Elders’ advice about children learning through everyday interaction shaped that work. The history also acknowledges inspiration from Māori language nests. This is a community institution’s account of rebuilding education; the page does not establish current proficiency outcomes for all Native Hawaiians.

Read the sources [1] ʻAha Pūnana Leo

05

Learning through care for land and water

Paepae o Heʻeia’s public collection explains how a coastal fishpond on Oʻahu uses a wall and managed water exchange to support aquatic life. Its education page describes students investigating water quality and other ecological questions while helping inform the organization’s management decisions. These accounts connect inherited environmental knowledge with contemporary learning at one place. Heʻeia’s story should not be generalized to every island, family or fishpond.

Read the sources [2] Paepae o Heʻeia

06

Understanding OHA as a particular institution

The Office of Hawaiian Affairs describes itself as a semi-autonomous state agency. Its account connects its creation with 1970s Native Hawaiian activism and the 1978 constitutional convention. It identifies advocacy, research, land management and support for community programs among its roles. Reading its own description helps distinguish a service and advocacy institution from the people as a whole. Its remit does not establish consensus on political futures or make OHA a sovereign Native Hawaiian government.

Read the sources [3] Office of Hawaiian Affairs

What needs further research

  • A fuller account needs Hawaiian-authored historical scholarship and original Kingdom-era documents, with island-specific histories.
  • Contemporary family voices, diaspora experiences, health and housing, and the diversity of political positions need stronger representation.
  • Legal program definitions, current law and recognition debates require separately dated specialist research; the 1993 resolution does not answer them all.
  • Learning outcomes, restoration results and present program availability have not been independently assessed.

Four substantive works/collections and one short supporting naming reference were inspected within recorded scopes on October 21, 2026. Paepae o Heʻeia pages count once. The guide is not promoted to a developed profile or an adequate initial introduction; no community review is implied. No generated images, copied photographs, restricted cultural content or precise site coordinates were used. The 1993 law was reviewed as text/OCR, not asserted as a full image-transcription audit.

Indigenous-ledʻAha Pūnana LeoSource 1

Our History ↗

Educators’ institutional account of rebuilding Hawaiian-medium education, beginning with organizing in 1983 and the first preschool in 1984. A valuable program history; historical policy claims and present outcomes still need independent comparison.

Inspection scope: Actual HTML history and timeline, lines 79–114. Photographs, linked courses, videos and private portals were not inspected.

The Fishpond and Education — Heʻeia public learning collection ↗

The community organization explains a coastal fishpond and connects its care with place-based ecological learning. The history and education pages are counted together as one public collection. Undated teaching schedules, output figures and ownership statements are not treated as verified current conditions.

Inspection scope: Actual Fishpond body, lines 54–76; Education introduction and charter-school learning account, lines 53–61. No restricted material, oral recordings, site geometry or photographs reused.

About the Office of Hawaiian Affairs ↗

OHA describes its state-agency role, origins in 1970s activism and work supporting Native Hawaiian wellbeing. Useful for understanding this particular institution; it is not a sovereign government speaking for every Native Hawaiian perspective. Staff totals and financial claims are omitted.

Inspection scope: Actual substantive About, vision, mission and overview text, lines 99–118. Linked film, program reports and current administrative rules were not reviewed.

Public Law 103–150: acknowledgment and apology for the overthrow of the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi ↗

Original 1993 federal resolution: historical recitals, apology, instrument-specific definition and non-settlement disclaimer. A dated primary instrument, not a complete history or determination of contemporary citizenship, sovereignty or remedies.

Inspection scope: Actual five-page PDF text/OCR read: 107 Stat. 1510–1514, all recitals and sections 1–3. This records text inspection, not a claimed page-image transcription audit.

Content checked October 21, 2026

Hawaiian Word of the Week: Maoli ↗

Brief university publication identifies Kānaka Maoli as the Indigenous people of Hawaiʻi through an attributed alumna’s reflection. Included for naming and orientation only; its brevity makes it supporting material rather than a substantive research-target source.

Inspection scope: Actual definition and attributed reflection, lines 34–49. Embedded video and linked dictionary were not reviewed.
